newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin operation delayed but doctors optimistic.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin operation delayed but doctors optimistic.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was given the go-ahead for heart surgery on Wednesday and doctors said they were confident the operation would be successful after another six to eight weeks of preparation.
Leading cardiologist Renat Akchurin, expected to head the team that will carry out the surgery, told a news conference the delay was needed to minimise the risk.
"If we operate now, I would say the chance is about 80 percent, but we hope that in six weeks the percentage would be close to 100," he said.
Akchurin later told reporters that Yeltsin, who has already agreed to the surgery, took this decision "courageously" and promised to carry out all of the doctors' recommendations.

The surgeon and other members of a team of doctors spent about two hours with the 65-year-old leader at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital assessing his condition. Yeltsin has been at the hospital since September 13.

Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who took part in the meeting, shared Akchurin's optimism. "After reviewing all facts I am very encouraged to tell you that the operation is needed, that it should provide excellent results," he said.
"There is no reason why the president should not be restored to full normal activity."
Yeltsin, who shook DeBakey's hand and called him "the patriarch of world surgery", had previously said that the surgery would take place at the end of this month.
Television footage from the hospital showed the president looking relaxed and smiling with a healthy glow to his face.

He looked much weaker on Tuesday at a meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, the president's constitutional substitute who is due to take over supreme power during the period of the operation.
Yeltsin joked that DeBakey, 88, had come to take a look at "what you might call, my sore point".
DeBakey said he would be permanently available to return to Moscow to advise his Russian colleagues.
Bill Clinton had asked him to make it his "first priority" and DeBakey said he had accepted the U.S. president's request.

The doctors set no firm date for the planned bypass operation, which is a relatively routine procedure, barring complications, and involved grafting in veins from the leg to relieve Yeltsin's clogged heart arteries.

DeBakey said there were some problems with "related general conditions" but the president's heart action had been getting stronger in the past month. He also dispelled rumours of kidney and liver problems, saying these organs were functioning.
The president's prolonged stay in hospital and his absence from public life have fuelled speculation about potentially destabilising power struggles brewing behind the scenes.
Kremlin officials have condemned the rumour-mongering as indecent and say the president is in full control of affairs of state, working on documents for up to 2-1/2 hours a day.

The undercurrent of instability in Russia was underlined on Wednesday by security chief Alexander Lebed, who told a Moscow newspaper that the government's failure to pay soldiers' wages could soon spark military uprisings.
"An armed mutiny may take place this autumn," the outspoken ex-paratroop general told the Vechernyaya Moskva daily.
In the interview he also condemned U.S. missile attacks on Iraq this month and warned that if that happened to Russia: "I would hit back instantly. With everything we've got."
In New York, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the remarks were "quite puzzling to us. We feel our relationship with Russia is on a very good footing."

Burns told reporters some of the remarks clashed with views expressed by other Russian leaders such as Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov. He suggested that the remarks might "need some explanation".
